items.label: f09-layer-probes
items.front: Doc 07's layer bisection: the cheap probe for each layer?
items.back: Frontend state: React Query devtools, localStorage. Transport: network tab, did the Authorization header go out. Authentication: decode the JWT, check iss, exp and kid against JWKS. Authorization: permissions claims vs the endpoint's policy. Service: Serilog logs. SQL: EF Database.Command logging at Information. Data: psql on RefreshTokens.

items.label: f05-pass-attribution
items.front: Doc 08's pass attribution: which findings did each review pass catch?
items.back: Trust boundary: F1, F2, F8, F17. Asset: F7, F9. State machine: F3, F4, F5, F11, F15. Negative space: F6, F10, F13, F14, F16 and the missing rotation audit. If your own review missed a cluster, that names the pass you under-practice, which is more useful than knowing the bug you missed.

items.label: f03-rotation-timeline
items.front: Refresh rotation with reuse detection, as a timeline?
items.back: login -> RT1, the first token of family F; use RT1 -> RT1 dead, RT2 issued in the same family (normal rotation); use RT2 -> RT2 dead, RT3 issued. Only the newest token of the family is live, so a dead token presented again is the reuse signal: someone kept a stale copy.

items.label: f08-test-risk-order
items.front: Doc 07: what to test first in this repo, in order of value?
items.back: Aim for invariant protection, not coverage. 1 Token lifecycle (rotation, replay, expiry, single-use codes): a regression silently breaks security. 2 Login state machine (lockout, MFA branching). 3 PKCE/redirect validation: one negative test per check. 4 Tenant scoping of queries. 5 UI behavior last.

items.label: f06-fix-leverage
items.front: Doc 08: how should a security review's fixes be ordered and grouped?
items.back: By leverage: ordering fixes is the senior deliverable, since anyone can list problems. Group findings by the fix that closes them, not by location; one pattern applied everywhere can close several findings and the whole class. Lead with a small, fully testable PR; file deployment-posture items until productionizing. Three PRs beat fourteen tickets.

items.label: f10-token-unit-costs
items.front: Doc 09: unit costs of token issuance and token lookups?
items.back: RSA PEM import + sign: about 1-5 ms for every JWT, twice per user login, each with its own key fetch. RSA-2048 keygen: tens to hundreds of ms, only after rotation or bootstrap. SHA-256 of a token: microseconds. Indexed point query on TokenHash or ClientId: sub-ms. Permissions join: one 3-join query per token pair.

items.label: f01-access-vs-id
items.front: Access token vs ID token in this provider?
items.back: Access token: for the API (authorization) with sub, tenant_id, client_id, scope and permissions claims. ID token: for the client (authentication) with email, name and the client's nonce, which binds it to the original request.

items.label: f07-test-seams
items.front: Doc 07: the seams that make this codebase testable?
items.back: IClock: a FakeClock makes lockout and expiry tests deterministic, no Thread.Sleep. IPasswordHasher: BCrypt at work factor 12 is slow on purpose, so login-heavy suites inject a cheap fake. RequestContext: construct it directly, no HTTP needed for service tests. `public partial class Program`: lets WebApplicationFactory<Program> host the app in-process.

items.label: f02-secret-storage
items.front: Storage form of the code flow's other secrets, besides the authorization code itself?
items.back: Password and client secret: BCrypt hashes. Refresh tokens and recovery codes: SHA-256 hashes. PKCE verifier: never stored. Signing key: plaintext PEM in the database, the outlier. TOTP secret: plaintext too, because the server needs it to compute codes.

items.label: f11-invariant-status
items.front: Doc 04's cross-flow invariants: the audit and permission promises, and their status?
items.back: Every security-relevant state change writes an audit event: currently false for key rotation and MFA enrollment. Permission changes take effect within one access-token lifetime (15 min), true because every refresh re-queries permissions. The senior skill is knowing which invariants are enforced and which are aspirational.

items.label: f04-sharp-edges
items.front: Four sharp edges of refresh rotation here?
items.back: Four spots where the refresh code relies on an ordering or an assumption. 1 Lines 192-197: the expiry test and the reuse test, and which of the two runs first. 2 Lines 211-227: the replacement is saved before the old token is marked rotated, with token issuance in between, so a crash there leaves two live tokens in one family. 3 Line 199: the IsActive check assumes requests arrive one at a time. 4 Lines 205-207: the User loaded for the new tokens, set against what authorize (line 37) and login check about a user. Doc 06 exercises 11 and 12 drill edges 3 and 4.

items.prompt: Two token requests load the same unconsumed authorization code at the same moment. What can happen?

choices.text: Both fail, because ConsumedAt is written before any validation
Both can receive tokens, with no concurrency token to stop them
The second gets a 409 from EF's optimistic concurrency check
The second's read of the code blocks until the first commits

choices: Both fail, because ConsumedAt is written before any validation
Both can receive tokens, with no concurrency token to stop them
The second gets a 409 from EF's optimistic concurrency check
The second's read of the code blocks until the first commits

items.explanation: Consumed is set in memory and saved at line 149; with no concurrency token both requests pass the IsActive check. Single-use holds only for replays after the first exchange committed.

items.prompt: Admin user search runs `Email.Contains(q) || DisplayName.ToLower().Contains(q)` on PostgreSQL. Per doc 09, why does it time out at a million users?

choices.text: EF evaluates Contains in memory after loading every user row first
The Email index is used, but DisplayName has no index to fall back on
Its leading-wildcard LIKE and LOWER calls defeat any B-tree index
Contains becomes a regex match that PostgreSQL re-plans per keystroke

choices: EF evaluates Contains in memory after loading every user row first
The Email index is used, but DisplayName has no index to fall back on
Its leading-wildcard LIKE and LOWER calls defeat any B-tree index
Contains becomes a regex match that PostgreSQL re-plans per keystroke

items.explanation: Doc 09 (lines 39-42): the query translates to `LIKE '%q%'` plus `LOWER(...)`, and "neither can use a B-tree index", so every search is a sequential scan: unnoticed at 10⁴ users, a timeout at 10⁶. The translation happens in SQL (no in-memory evaluation, no regex), and the fix ladder starts with a sargable prefix match (StartsWith), then a pg_trgm GIN index.

items.prompt: You add Testcontainers-based tests to NetAuth0.IntegrationTests and they pass on your machine. Per doc 07, why do they not protect anything yet?

choices.text: The project lacks the Mvc.Testing and Testcontainers packages
CI runs only the UnitTests project, so a CI step must be added
CI runs every test project but skips any test that needs Docker
Testcontainers cannot start Docker on ubuntu-latest GitHub runners

choices: The project lacks the Mvc.Testing and Testcontainers packages
CI runs only the UnitTests project, so a CI step must be added
CI runs every test project but skips any test that needs Docker
Testcontainers cannot start Docker on ubuntu-latest GitHub runners

items.explanation: Doc 07 (lines 29-43): "CI runs exactly one test command", `dotnet test tests/NetAuth0.UnitTests/...` (ci.yml:18). IntegrationTests already has the packages but no CI step, so "nothing you put in IntegrationTests is protected until someone adds a CI step for it"; that step needs Docker, which ubuntu-latest runners have. "A test that no pipeline runs is documentation, not protection."

items.prompt: RT1 was already rotated into RT2 and has not expired yet. Someone presents RT1 again. What happens?

choices.text: Every token in RT1's family is marked reused and revoked
Only RT1 is rejected, and RT2 keeps working for its holder
RT1 is accepted once more, since it has not yet expired
RT2 is revoked, and RT1 is given a fresh child token

choices: Every token in RT1's family is marked reused and revoked
Only RT1 is rejected, and RT2 keeps working for its holder
RT1 is accepted once more, since it has not yet expired
RT2 is revoked, and RT1 is given a fresh child token

items.explanation: A dead token (ReplacedById set) means someone holds a stale copy; RevokeFamilyForReuseAsync marks the whole family reused+revoked and audits refresh_token.reuse_detected.

items.prompt: A stolen refresh token is replayed after it has already expired. What does ExchangeRefreshTokenAsync do?

choices.text: It revokes the whole family and audits reuse_detected for the user
That one token is revoked quietly, without a family revocation
It blocks the user until an admin unlocks the account
It rotates the token, since refresh expiry is not checked

choices: It revokes the whole family and audits reuse_detected for the user
That one token is revoked quietly, without a family revocation
It blocks the user until an admin unlocks the account
It rotates the token, since refresh expiry is not checked

items.explanation: Expiry is checked before reuse (lines 192-197): an expired token is revoked and the request fails, without tripping the reuse alarm.

items.prompt: An attacker already knows a user's password and starts guessing TOTP codes at login. Per finding F3, what limits them?

choices.text: Only the per-IP limiter, since failed codes never count toward lockout
A per-account counter of wrong codes that slows each next attempt
Nothing at all, since the IP limiter does not cover the MFA step
A lockout after repeated bad codes, the same as for bad passwords

choices: Only the per-IP limiter, since failed codes never count toward lockout
A per-account counter of wrong codes that slows each next attempt
Nothing at all, since the IP limiter does not cover the MFA step
A lockout after repeated bad codes, the same as for bad passwords

items.explanation: F3 (line 38): MFA failures bypass RegisterFailure, so there is no per-account counter and no lockout, and `out _` discards the matched time step, so there is no per-step replay rejection. "Only the per-IP 20/min limiter stands between a password-holder and the 10⁶ code space." IdentityService.cs:80-84 audits the MFA failure and throws without calling RegisterFailure.

items.prompt: Per finding F8, how does MFA enrollment verification find the enrollment it is about to verify?

choices.text: By the caller's user ID, so only their own pending enrollment
By enrollment ID and the user ID taken from the caller's token
By enrollment ID within the tenant named in the caller's claims
By enrollment ID alone, without comparing the caller to its owner

choices: By the caller's user ID, so only their own pending enrollment
By enrollment ID and the user ID taken from the caller's token
By enrollment ID within the tenant named in the caller's claims
By enrollment ID alone, without comparing the caller to its owner

items.explanation: F8 (line 43): "Verification looks up by enrollment ID only; caller's identity never checked", part of a pattern of unscoped lookups. IdentityService.cs:116 loads the row with `x.Id == request.EnrollmentId` and nothing else, so no user or tenant from the caller's token takes part.

items.prompt: Why does the provider sign with RS256 and not HS256?

choices.text: HS256 tokens cannot carry the kid header needed for rotation
RS256 tokens are smaller and cheaper to send on every call
With HS256, each verifier would hold a key able to sign
ASP.NET Core JwtBearer has no support for HS256 at all

choices: HS256 tokens cannot carry the kid header needed for rotation
RS256 tokens are smaller and cheaper to send on every call
With HS256, each verifier would hold a key able to sign
ASP.NET Core JwtBearer has no support for HS256 at all

items.explanation: HS256 is symmetric, so any resource server could forge tokens; with RS256 the private key stays with the provider and anyone can verify with the public key.

items.prompt: A client registered https://app.example/cb, and an authorize request uses https://app.example/cb/extra. What happens?

choices.text: It is refused, since only an exact Ordinal match is accepted
It is accepted, since the host app.example is the same in both
It is refused, but only when the client is a public SPA client
It is accepted, as the registered URI is a prefix of the request

choices: It is refused, since only an exact Ordinal match is accepted
It is accepted, since the host app.example is the same in both
It is refused, but only when the client is a public SPA client
It is accepted, as the registered URI is a prefix of the request

items.explanation: ValidateRedirectUri requires string.Equals(x.Uri, redirectUri, StringComparison.Ordinal) for some registered URI; no prefix or wildcard matching, as RFC 9700 requires.

items.prompt: The public-auth limiter partitions on raw RemoteIpAddress, and the API is exposed directly with no proxy in front. Per finding F12, what defeats it?

choices.text: Switching client_id per attempt, since buckets are kept per client
An attacker rotating source IPs, since each address gets its own bucket
Varying the email per attempt, since buckets are kept per account
A forged X-Forwarded-For header, which it reads as the client address

choices: Switching client_id per attempt, since buckets are kept per client
An attacker rotating source IPs, since each address gets its own bucket
Varying the email per attempt, since buckets are kept per account
A forged X-Forwarded-For header, which it reads as the client address

items.explanation: F12 (line 47): the limiter is "keyed on raw `RemoteIpAddress`"; behind a proxy everyone shares one bucket, and "without one, attacker IP rotation defeats it." "No forwarded-headers config exists", so X-Forwarded-For is never read, and Program.cs:75-76 partitions on the connection address only, not on the account or the client.

items.prompt: An attacker copies an authorization code from a log. Why can't they redeem it for a public SPA client?

choices.text: They lack the code_verifier that the stored challenge was made from
The code is bound to the attacker's IP address at authorize time
The token endpoint also needs the user's password with the code
Codes are encrypted with the client secret before they are sent

choices: They lack the code_verifier that the stored challenge was made from
The code is bound to the attacker's IP address at authorize time
The token endpoint also needs the user's password with the code
Codes are encrypted with the client secret before they are sent

items.explanation: PKCE: the client sent SHA256(verifier) as code_challenge; at exchange the server re-hashes the presented verifier and compares in constant time. The verifier never left the legitimate client.

items.prompt: An admin-page 403 is traced to a permission string that drifted between the seeded claims and the endpoint policy. Per doc 07, where does the regression test go?

choices.text: At the layer where the bug lived, not the layer it surfaced in
In the UI, end to end, so that one test covers every layer at once
At the layer where it surfaced, since that is what the user saw
At every layer it crossed, with one regression test for each layer

choices: At the layer where the bug lived, not the layer it surfaced in
In the UI, end to end, so that one test covers every layer at once
At the layer where it surfaced, since that is what the user saw
At every layer it crossed, with one regression test for each layer

items.explanation: Doc 07 (lines 272-273): "Root cause found → write the regression test at the layer the bug lived in, not the layer it surfaced in." Here the 403 surfaced in the admin UI, but the drift lives in the claim and policy strings, so that is where the test belongs; neither a UI test nor one test per layer is what the playbook asks for.

items.prompt: A user is blocked after they logged in. Their client then uses a live refresh token. What is the result?

choices.text: New tokens are issued, since refresh never checks IsBlocked
It succeeds, but the new access token has no permissions
It fails with "User is blocked." as on the authorize path
The whole token family is revoked for the blocked user right away

choices: New tokens are issued, since refresh never checks IsBlocked
It succeeds, but the new access token has no permissions
It fails with "User is blocked." as on the authorize path
The whole token family is revoked for the blocked user right away

items.explanation: Lines 205-207 load the User but never look at IsBlocked, while authorize (line 37) and login both check it. A gym exercise in doc 06.

items.prompt: How does the provider store an authorization code it has just minted?

choices.text: In plaintext, so that the token endpoint can compare it directly
As a signed JWT, so that the server never needs to store it
As a SHA-256 hash that expires in 5 minutes and is single-use
As a BCrypt hash, exactly like passwords and client secrets

choices: In plaintext, so that the token endpoint can compare it directly
As a signed JWT, so that the server never needs to store it
As a SHA-256 hash that expires in 5 minutes and is single-use
As a BCrypt hash, exactly like passwords and client secrets

items.explanation: 32 random bytes, base64url; the row stores secrets.Sha256Base64Url(code) with clock.UtcNow.AddMinutes(5), and IsActive requires ConsumedAt to be null.

items.prompt: Unknown-user and wrong-password logins both return "Invalid credentials." Per finding F11, how can an attacker still tell which emails have accounts?

choices.text: Real users' failures are slower, but only after their account locks
Unknown users run BCrypt twice, so their failures return slower
Unknown users skip the BCrypt verify, so their failures return faster
Unknown users get a different message once the tenant slug is valid

choices: Real users' failures are slower, but only after their account locks
Unknown users run BCrypt twice, so their failures return slower
Unknown users skip the BCrypt verify, so their failures return faster
Unknown users get a different message once the tenant slug is valid

items.explanation: F11 (line 46): "Unknown-user login skips the BCrypt verify (work factor 12, hundreds of ms); uniform message, non-uniform latency." So the timing, not the text, separates real accounts. A locked or blocked account gets its own message "before any password check" (IdentityService.cs:58-61), so locking does not make a failure slower.

items.prompt: Why does doc 07 tell you to skip mocking IAppDbContext in this repo's service tests?

choices.text: A mocked DbSet rejects LINQ that PostgreSQL would happily translate
Service tests should be pure unit tests that use no database at all
WebApplicationFactory tests already cover every query end to end
The SQL translation is part of what the service test must check

choices: A mocked DbSet rejects LINQ that PostgreSQL would happily translate
Service tests should be pure unit tests that use no database at all
WebApplicationFactory tests already cover every query end to end
The SQL translation is part of what the service test must check

items.explanation: Doc 07 (lines 21-25): the shape mix is "mostly service-level tests against a real database (EF + PostgreSQL via Testcontainers)" and only "a few WebApplicationFactory tests for the HTTP contract". Skip mocking IAppDbContext because "mocked DbSet LINQ lies to you; the SQL translation is part of what you're testing": the mock is more permissive than the database, not stricter.

items.prompt: Why can't a standard OAuth client library tell an invalid_grant failure from an invalid_client failure at this provider's token endpoint?

choices.text: Spec-shaped errors are sent, but production strips the error field
Every failure becomes a generic 400 that is not shaped per RFC 6749
Both errors return 401, and only the WWW-Authenticate header differs
Both errors become a 500 whose body hides the original exception

choices: Spec-shaped errors are sent, but production strips the error field
Every failure becomes a generic 400 that is not shaped per RFC 6749
Both errors return 401, and only the WWW-Authenticate header differs
Both errors become a 500 whose body hides the original exception

items.explanation: F10 (line 45): error handling "collapses everything to 400" and leaks exception messages in Development; "OAuth errors are not RFC 6749-shaped, so client libraries can't distinguish `invalid_grant` from `invalid_client`." Program.cs:113-123 is one exception handler that always answers statusCode 400 with a generic "Request failed" problem.

items.prompt: Why does CreateAuthorizationCodeAsync accept only response_type=code?

choices.text: OIDC discovery cannot advertise more than one response type
PKCE cannot be combined with any other response_type value
The token endpoint is too slow to answer browsers directly
The implicit flow put tokens in URL fragments that leak

choices: OIDC discovery cannot advertise more than one response type
PKCE cannot be combined with any other response_type value
The token endpoint is too slow to answer browsers directly
The implicit flow put tokens in URL fragments that leak

items.explanation: The legacy implicit flow (token) returned tokens in URL fragments, which leak via browser history and Referer headers; the code flow returns only a short-lived code.

items.prompt: A user reports being logged out of everything. Which hypothesis does doc 07's playbook check first, and with what probe?

choices.text: Key rotation: check whether the token's kid is still served by JWKS
Admin force-logout: query the audit table for the force-logout event
Natural expiry: compare the ExpiresAt values of the user's tokens
Replay detection fired: query the audit table for reuse_detected

choices: Key rotation: check whether the token's kid is still served by JWKS
Admin force-logout: query the audit table for the force-logout event
Natural expiry: compare the ExpiresAt values of the user's tokens
Replay detection fired: query the audit table for reuse_detected

items.explanation: Doc 07 (lines 277-282) ranks hypotheses "by prior probability, cheapest probe first": (a) replay detection fired, so query audit for `refresh_token.reuse_detected` (one SQL query, which also gives the IP); (b) admin force-logout, audit again; (c) natural expiry, compare ExpiresAt values. Key rotation is not one of the three; the doc mentions it only because its missing audit event would hide a rotation-caused mass logout.

items.prompt: Why must redirect_uri be presented again at the token exchange, after authorize already validated it?

choices.text: The token response is posted to that URI rather than to the caller
The authorize step never validated the redirect in the first place
It stands in for the client secret when a client is confidential
It proves the code is redeemed for the redirect it was issued to

choices: The token response is posted to that URI rather than to the caller
The authorize step never validated the redirect in the first place
It stands in for the client secret when a client is confidential
It proves the code is redeemed for the redirect it was issued to

items.explanation: RFC 6749 4.1.3 binding: comparing it with the stored code.RedirectUri blocks mix-up attacks where a code issued under one redirect is redeemed claiming another.

items.prompt: Doc 08's review runs four passes: trust boundary, asset, state machine, negative space. Why trust boundaries first and negative space last?

choices.text: The asset pass needs the endpoint list that the trust pass produces
Negative space is the cheapest pass, so it is left for the time remaining
Trust boundaries need no domain knowledge; negative space needs all of it
Trust-boundary bugs are always the most severe, so they are found first

choices: The asset pass needs the endpoint list that the trust pass produces
Negative space is the cheapest pass, so it is left for the time remaining
Trust boundaries need no domain knowledge; negative space needs all of it
Trust-boundary bugs are always the most severe, so they are found first

items.explanation: Doc 08 (lines 23-24): "trust boundaries first because they require zero domain knowledge, negative space last because it requires all of it." The order follows how much you must understand about the system, not severity or a hand-off between passes, and the negative-space pass is called the hardest one (line 20), not the cheapest.

items.prompt: Why is accepting code_challenge_method=plain a weakness in this provider?

choices.text: With plain, the token endpoint skips the redirect_uri comparison
With plain, codes stay valid for 5 hours instead of 5 minutes
With plain, the challenge is written unhashed to the audit log
With plain, anyone who sees the challenge holds the verifier

choices: With plain, the token endpoint skips the redirect_uri comparison
With plain, codes stay valid for 5 hours instead of 5 minutes
With plain, the challenge is written unhashed to the audit log
With plain, anyone who sees the challenge holds the verifier

items.explanation: For plain the expected challenge is the raw verifier itself, so anyone who saw the challenge can redeem the code. The RFC permits it; modern policy rejects it.

items.prompt: The API sets ValidateAudience = false. What does that allow?

choices.text: A token for any client passes, if its permission claims fit
Tokens signed by some other issuer pass validation without a check
Expired tokens are accepted with no time limit at all
Unsigned tokens using alg none get through to [Authorize] endpoints

choices: A token for any client passes, if its permission claims fit
Tokens signed by some other issuer pass validation without a check
Expired tokens are accepted with no time limit at all
Unsigned tokens using alg none get through to [Authorize] endpoints

items.explanation: Signature, issuer and lifetime are validated; audience is not, so the token's intended client is ignored and only permission claims decide.

items.prompt: A confidential client's refresh token is stolen. Per finding F5, what else must the attacker send to the token endpoint to use it?

choices.text: Only the public client_id, because omitting the secret skips its check
The original code_verifier, which refresh re-checks against PKCE
The client secret too, which is checked on every refresh request
A live access token, since refresh needs an active bearer session

choices: Only the public client_id, because omitting the secret skips its check
The original code_verifier, which refresh re-checks against PKCE
The client secret too, which is checked on every refresh request
A live access token, since refresh needs an active bearer session

items.explanation: F5 (line 40): the secret is "verified only when the request volunteers one", so a "stolen refresh token + public client_id suffices". OAuthService.cs:183-186 calls ValidateClientSecretIfRequiredAsync only inside `if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(request.ClientSecret))`: leaving the secret out skips the check instead of failing it.

items.prompt: A user with TOTP enabled loses their phone but still has the recovery codes shown at enrollment. Per finding F6, what happens?

choices.text: They can redeem a code, but only after an admin unblocks the account
They enter a code in place of the TOTP, and that code is then consumed
They stay locked out, because no login path ever redeems a recovery code
They log in once with a recovery code, and MFA is then reset for them

choices: They can redeem a code, but only after an admin unblocks the account
They enter a code in place of the TOTP, and that code is then consumed
They stay locked out, because no login path ever redeems a recovery code
They log in once with a recovery code, and MFA is then reset for them

items.explanation: F6 (line 41): recovery codes are "generated and stored; no redemption path exists" (`RecoveryCode.Use` has no callers). "Lost authenticator = permanent lockout, while the API advertises recovery." IdentityService.cs:104-108 only creates and hashes the codes at enrollment.

items.prompt: Login succeeds, but the admin pages fail. In doc 07's playbook, what is the first question to ask, and why?

choices.text: Is the user's role seeded, since empty permissions are the usual cause
Is it 401 or 403, since that splits authentication from authorization
Is the API reachable, since the network tab shows whether calls fail
Is the JWT expired, since its 15-minute lifetime is the usual cause

choices: Is the user's role seeded, since empty permissions are the usual cause
Is it 401 or 403, since that splits authentication from authorization
Is the API reachable, since the network tab shows whether calls fail
Is the JWT expired, since its 15-minute lifetime is the usual cause

items.explanation: Doc 07's worked scenario (lines 259-262): step 1 is "401 vs 403, which?" 401 is authentication (token absent or invalid) and 403 is authorization (valid token, missing claim); "this one question halves the search space." Checking expiry and decoding permissions come later (steps 3 and 4), on the branch the first answer selects.

items.prompt: Just after a signing-key rotation, a token signed a minute earlier still validates. Why?

choices.text: Rotation only takes effect after the API process restarts
JwtBearer skips the signature check for very recent tokens
The new key is derived from the old one, so both verify it
JWKS still serves keys retired within the last 7 days

choices: Rotation only takes effect after the API process restarts
JwtBearer skips the signature check for very recent tokens
The new key is derived from the old one, so both verify it
JWKS still serves keys retired within the last 7 days

items.explanation: GetJwksAsync returns keys with RetiredAt null or within the last 7 days; the token's kid selects the old public key. The grace window must exceed the longest token lifetime.
